statement: Two cars each drive 240 km. Car P drives the first half of the distance at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Car Q drives at 40 km/h for the first half of its travel time and at 60 km/h for the second half. They start together. How many minutes before P does Q arrive?

choices.misconception: I thought both cars average 50 km/h, because 50 is halfway between 40 and 60.
I found the gap as 0.2 hours and read it as 20 minutes.
I gave car P's average speed, 48 km/h, instead of the difference in time.
I thought car Q takes 240 / 60 = 4 hours, as if it drove at 60 km/h all the way, so the gap came out as 1 hour.

hints: Work out each car's total time separately.
Equal times at two speeds give the simple average speed, but equal distances do not, because the car spends longer at the slower speed. Compute each car's total time directly.
Car P takes 120/40 + 120/60 hours. Car Q averages 50 km/h.

solutions.reliable: Car P: 120 km at 40 km/h takes 3 hours and 120 km at 60 km/h takes 2 hours, so 5 hours in all. Car Q spends equal times at 40 and 60 km/h, so its average speed is 50 km/h and it takes 240 / 50 = 4.8 hours. The difference is 0.2 hours, which is 0.2 x 60 = 12 minutes. The transferable idea: average speed is total distance over total time, and it equals the simple average of two speeds only when the times are equal.

whyOnTest: Averaging the two speeds works for car Q but not for car P, and the question probes exactly that difference, plus a decimal-hours trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
